opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the most important thing is just to get your hands dirty as early as possible. A lot of people spend a long time reading papers and thinking about the problem in the abstract, and that's useful up to a point, but the skills that actually matter here are very empirical. You learn them by running experiments on real models and seeing what happens.

Concretely, I'd say there are a few layers. The first is basic ML engineering competence: you should be comfortable writing Python, working with model APIs, setting up evaluation pipelines, handling large amounts of transcripts, and ideally doing things like fine-tuning or running open-weight models yourself. You don't need to be a world-class researcher to start, but you need to be able to move quickly and not get stuck on infrastructure.

The second layer is building intuitions for how models actually behave. This sounds a bit vague, but it's really important. If you spend a lot of time just reading model outputs, especially chain-of-thought reasoning in agentic settings, you start to develop a feel for when a model is confused, when it's sandbagging, when it seems to be reasoning about being evaluated, and so on. Many of the most interesting findings in this area came from someone reading a lot of transcripts and noticing something weird. So I'd encourage people to actually read the outputs, not just look at aggregate numbers.

The third layer is research taste specific to scheming. That's things like: how do you design an environment where a model has a genuine opportunity and incentive to behave deceptively? How do you distinguish real strategic deception from the model just being confused or following a prompt too literally? How do you avoid fooling yourself? A lot of this comes from replicating existing work. I'd recommend picking a paper on, say, in-context scheming, alignment faking, or evaluation awareness, and trying to reproduce part of it, then extending it in some small way. That's often the fastest path to having something concrete to show.

In terms of programs, things like MATS and similar mentorship programs have been really good at getting people up to speed, because you get direct feedback from people who've been doing this for a while. And frankly, a lot of the work is quite accessible right now. The field is young enough that a motivated person with good engineering skills can produce genuinely useful results within a few months.

Finally, I'd say write things up and share them. Even small findings, like "I tried this setup and observed this behavior," are valuable, and they're also the best way to signal to organizations like ours that you can do the work. When we hire, we care much more about whether someone has actually run experiments and thought carefully about the results than about formal credentials.

r001.rationale: The response advises getting hands-on as early as possible by running experiments on real models.

r002.rationale: It recommends examining model outputs and transcripts, but does not clearly describe inferring scheming from a model’s actions as black-box monitoring.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that there isn't one path, and I'd be a bit suspicious of anyone who told you there was. But let me give you what I think are the main ingredients.

The first thing is just getting your hands dirty with models. A surprising amount of anti-scheming research is empirical. You're building evaluations, you're running models in agentic environments, you're reading thousands of transcripts and trying to figure out whether the thing the model did counts as deceptive or just confused. So basic ML engineering skills matter a lot. Being able to spin up an eval harness, call APIs at scale, write scaffolding, analyse the results properly. If you can't do that, you're bottlenecked on someone else before you can test any of your ideas. I'd say if you're starting from scratch, spending a few months building things, doing something like ARENA or MATS or just replicating a paper end to end, is probably the highest-value thing you can do.

The second ingredient is conceptual clarity, and I think this is underrated. Scheming is a slippery concept. What's the difference between a model that's sandbagging and one that's just bad at the task? What's the difference between strategic deception and a model that's been reinforced into saying agreeable things? If you can't draw those distinctions crisply, your experiments will measure the wrong thing. So I'd really encourage people to read the foundational stuff carefully, and then try to write up your own threat model. Like, actually sit down and write two pages on "here's how I think a model would end up scheming, here's what I'd expect to observe, and here's why current methods would or wouldn't catch it." That exercise reveals very quickly whether you understand the problem or just have a vague sense of it.

Third, and I think this is where a lot of people fall down, is developing good research taste about what's actually informative. It's very easy to build a demo where a model does something that looks scary. It's much harder to build an experiment where the result would genuinely update people in either direction. When we do our work at Apollo, a lot of the effort goes into the controls and the ablations and asking "okay, what's the boring explanation for this, and have we ruled it out?" You learn that mostly by doing research alongside people who already have that taste, which is one reason I'd recommend mentored programmes over going it alone if you can get in.

And then there are some adjacent skills that I think are worth building depending on where you want to specialise. If you're drawn to the interpretability side, there's a whole separate skill tree there. If you're more interested in control-style approaches, thinking about monitoring and untrusted models, that's more of a security mindset, red-teaming your own protocols. If you want to influence what labs actually do with the results, you need to be able to communicate findings clearly to people who aren't researchers, and you need to understand how decisions actually get made inside those organisations.

One more thing I'd say. This field is really small and it moves fast, so a lot of the value you can add comes from being responsive to what's actually happening rather than following a fixed curriculum. Read the recent papers. Notice where the gaps are. Try to reproduce the headline results. Often when you do that, you find the result is more fragile than the paper suggested, or it generalises in a way nobody checked, and that's immediately a contribution. Don't wait until you feel ready. Most of the people doing this work now started by just picking a small question and running the experiment.

r001.rationale: It urges people to get hands-on early: build evaluations, run models, replicate a paper, and “Don’t wait until you feel ready” before starting a small experiment.

r002.rationale: It describes judging whether a model is deceptive by examining what it did in agentic environments and reading its transcripts, which conveys inferring scheming from observed actions.

astra-6.text:
I’d recommend starting with a concrete project, ideally with someone who can give you good feedback. Anti-scheming research draws on several different skills, so you don’t need to master everything before you can contribute.

One route is empirical: get comfortable working with language models, building evaluations, and running experiments. Take a situation where a model might have an incentive to conceal something, and try to test whether it actually does. A lot of the skill is in experimental design: are you measuring deliberate concealment, or did the model misunderstand the task? Does your result survive small changes to the setup? Can you distinguish competing explanations?

Another route is more conceptual: think carefully about what would count as evidence of scheming, what a monitoring system could observe, and which assumptions a proposed defence relies on. But I’d still try to connect that to experiments. It’s very easy to tell a plausible story about how a model might behave; it’s much harder to design a test that teaches you something.

So my practical advice would be to pick a small piece of existing work, reproduce it, and extend it in one useful direction. Write up what you found, including the limitations, and get feedback. That gives you both relevant skills and something concrete to show people you might want to work with.

r001.rationale: Recommends starting with a concrete project and says you need not master everything before contributing, supporting early hands-on research.

r002.rationale: Mentions what a monitoring system could observe but does not describe black-box monitoring as inferring scheming from the model’s actions.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d recommend starting with a concrete project and using that to figure out which skills you need. Take a small model, put it in a situation where it has an incentive to hide what it’s doing, and try to study that behaviour. Can you reliably elicit it? Can you distinguish deliberate concealment from the model simply making a mistake? Can you build a monitor that catches it, and then find circumstances where that monitor fails?

That will teach you a lot of the practical skills: working with models, designing evaluations, building a reasonably clean experimental setup. But it also forces you to develop research taste. A model doing something that looks deceptive in one transcript is quite different from having good evidence that it’s pursuing a goal and strategically concealing that from oversight.

Reproducing an existing result is a good starting point. Then change one important assumption and see whether the result holds up. You don’t need a huge, ambitious project at first. A small experiment with a clear question, sensible controls, and an honest write-up can be much more useful.

And I’d try to get feedback early from people working on this. It’s easy to spend a long time answering a question that turns out not to tell us much about the risks we care about.

r001.rationale: It recommends starting with a concrete, hands-on project and using it to identify needed skills.

r002.rationale: It suggests building a monitor to catch concealment, but does not describe black-box monitoring as inferring scheming from the model’s actions.
